subject: science
topic: Modern light pollution is fundamentally altering human circadian gene expression
angle: While blue light specifically increases neuronal gene expression in mice and light exposure generally disrupts human circadian rhythms, the evidence also shows that even red light and very low light levels can trigger circadian responses.
title: The Light You Don't See

hooks.text: Does your room stay dark enough for your genes?
You think blue light is the only problem. The evidence shows red light matters too.
You are letting light pollution rewrite your internal clock.
A faint red glow hits your eyelids.

reveal.headline: Red light and low light also trigger circadian responses.
reveal.body: The evidence shows that your circadian rhythm reacts to more than just blue light. Even the longest wavelengths and very low light levels at night can impact your internal clock.

explain.headline: Light alters your internal clock.
explain.body: Mistimed light exposure is linked to disruptions in your circadian rhythm. This includes changes in the phase of melatonin levels. Even exposure with your eyes closed can trigger a response.

matters.headline: Your environment is never fully dark.
matters.body: That may be why you feel restless even in a dim room. Modern light pollution may be constantly signaling your genes to stay active, regardless of the color of the light.

example.headline: A street lamp outside your window.
example.body: You sleep in a room with the curtains drawn. A faint glow from the street filters through the fabric, hitting your skin and eyes while you rest.

question.headline: Is your room ever truly dark?
question.body: Think about what light reaches you at night.

stat.label: low light levels at night linked to a circadian response

claims.text: Exposure to low light levels (5-10 lux) at night when sleeping with eyes closed is linked to a circadian response.
claims.quote: exposure to low light levels (5-10 lux) at night when sleeping with eyes closed induced a circadian response.

claims.text: Even the longest wavelengths (631 nm, red) and intermittent light exposures are linked to circadian resetting responses.
claims.quote: In addition, even the longest wavelengths (631 nm, red) and intermittent light exposures induced circadian resetting responses

claims.text: Exposing mouse cortical cultures to as short as 1 h of blue light causes an increase in the expression of neuronal activity-regulated genes.
claims.quote: We found that exposing these cultures to as short as 1 h of blue light, but not red or green light, results in an increase in the expression of neuronal activity-regulated genes.

claims.text: Blue light can be used to switch light-inducible and repressible systems between ON- and OFF-states in bacteria.
claims.quote: We show that both light-inducible and repressible system can function in parallel with high spatial precision in a single cell and can be switched stably between ON- and OFF-states by repetitive pulses of blue light.

claims.text: Mistimed light exposure is linked to disruptions in the human circadian rhythm.
claims.quote: Findings from a number of studies suggest that mistimed light exposure disrupts the circadian rhythm in humans, potentially causing further health impacts.

claims.text: Light exposure in the evening, at night and in the morning is linked to changes in the circadian phase of melatonin levels.
claims.quote: Light exposure in the evening, at night and in the morning affected the circadian phase of melatonin levels.

verdict: The sources confirm that light exposure impacts human circadian rhythms and gene expression, but they also show that these effects are not exclusive to blue light.
caveat: The evidence regarding human gene expression is limited to observational links, while specific gene expression changes were only demonstrated in mouse cultures and bacteria.
caption:
Modern light pollution is fundamentally altering your internal biology. 

Research shows that mistimed light exposure is linked to disruptions in human circadian rhythms and melatonin levels. While some studies show specific gene changes in mouse cultures, the evidence for humans is currently limited to observational links. 

How much light reaches your bedroom at night?
